The thesis
goal of Plan 42 is to change ownership of the child from the parents and place it more on the village, the way I was "taught"...

— Matthew Nahas, founder

Age-seven version · Start here

Plan 42c

Here is the plan as a short story. It starts with schools on Earth. It ends near another star.

Project 84: the dummies guide ↗
1

First, we build new cities.

There are 260 of them to start. Most are on land. They are big school cities for teens. Grown-ups help teach, cook, heal, fix and build. A few cities are in the sea. They help clean and care for the ocean.

2

All the schools help each other.

learn to apply maths, science and reading that they should have already learned. They can also learn to grow food, make things and care for a city. Every school has its own name and culture. But they share ideas and work as one team.

3

Good work earns credits.

Students get credits when they learn and help. The credits work inside the school cities. They are like points for real work. People cannot buy and sell them like toys. When school is done, the work becomes part of the student's record and reward.

4

The AI holds a clipboard.

It checks the lists. It finds mistakes. It gives reminders. It can help a student learn in a new way. But it is not the boss. People make the big choices. Grown-up students check the AI too.

5

Then we take one careful step into space.

Earth comes first. Next is the Moon. Then comes Jupiter. Much later, people may travel to Alpha Centauri. A small station at Barnard's Star can watch and learn. The whole trip may take 28,000 years. That is okay. Big trips begin with one good first step.

Build a school. Learn together. Help Earth. Then use what we learned to go farther.

Plain-language version · More detail

Plan 42b

This is Plan #42 in simpler words. It is not a smaller plan. It is the same big idea, explained so you can understand the whole thing without reading every estimate and engineering note.

01

Build 261 cities.

There would be 257 cities on land. Each one would be a home and school for about 3 million people ages 14–19, with about 300,000 adults helping. At least four more cities would be built in the ocean. Nobody would live in those ocean cities. Their job would be to help repair the sea.

02

Connect the schools.

The 257 land cities would work as one school network. Countries would help students get ready before they arrive. Students would learn regular subjects, job skills and how to help run a city. Each school could keep its own name and culture while sharing the same basic system.

03

Give credit for real work.

Students would earn class credits for learning, service and useful work. The credits could be used only inside the 257 land cities. When a student leaves, the school would buy the credits back and turn completed work into a record and reward. The credits could not be traded or sold to other people.

04

Use AI as a checker, not a boss.

The AI would keep records, find problems, balance supplies, give reminders and help each student learn. It could flag a mistake, but it could not punish someone or make the final choice. People would decide grades, discipline, laws and rights. Graduates would check the AI's work.

05

Use Earth to practice for space.

The Earth cities would test how large groups can learn, build and live together. If the model works, the next steps would be Luna, Jupiter and then Alpha Centauri over about 28,000 years. A station at Barnard's Star would gather information along the way. Each step would help prove the next one.

EarthBuild and test the city network.
LunaBuild the first cities away from Earth.
JupiterLearn to live much farther from home.
Alpha CentauriCarry the model to another star.

What is the point?

Give young people a strong education, build useful cities, make food and energy systems that can last, help the ocean, and practice the skills humanity would need to live beyond Earth.

Is it ready to build?

No. It is still a plan. The numbers are rough, and hard questions about money, law, safety and engineering still need real answers. The simple version does not hide that.

POINT SYSTEM / BONUS ECONOMY

Do good here. Spend it there.

Project 42 adds a bonus economy to New Eden: real-world good deeds earn digital points for use in its virtual world. Building schools, volunteering and other pro-social work create value without turning people into a leaderboard.

01 · Real world Do the good.

Help build a school, volunteer, repair something shared or contribute another verified act that helps people and place.

→
02 · The point Earn plankton.

Plankton is the small digital unit in the Project 84 currency family. Enough plankton stacks up to Koins.

→
03 · Virtual world Spend the bonus.

The deed happens in the real world. The reward is used in New Eden’s virtual world.

What earns points

  • Build what people needSchools and other useful shared infrastructure count.
  • Give timeVolunteering turns service into a visible, earned bonus.
  • Act for the common goodOther verified pro-social work can earn points too.

How the system behaves

  • Earned and visible, never rankedThink scout merit badges, football helmet stickers or gold stars on an essay: recognition without hierarchy.
  • Additive, not punitiveThe system records what someone adds. It does not run on deductions, debt or punishment.
  • Sharing over owningThe reward lives inside a replacement economy built to make access and contribution matter more than possession.
  • Bonus, not human worthPlankton and Koins recognize good acts. They do not price people or create rank.

Real-world good creates virtual freedom. The score only adds.

Plan #42 and Project 42 are interchangeable names for the same project. It is now a 261-site project: 257 land cities sized for today's roughly 770 million 14–19-year-olds and 77 million supporting adults, plus at least four additive ocean cities dedicated to healing the sea. A separate 810-row planning set offers nonbinding land-site suggestions—not a project map or mandate.

01 / THE MODEL

One land unit. A 261-site project.

Each of the project's 257 land cities is planned for roughly 3.3 million people: 3 million residents aged 14–19 and 300,000 supporting adults aged 30+. Together they match today's global youth cohort. At least four uninhabited ocean cities are additive, bringing the current project total to 261 without changing the land-cohort math.

The 257-land-city rollout

four overlapping land waves · years 1–24

Four growing, pipelined waves

  1. Wave 1 · volunteer pilots · ~20 sites

    Years 1–6. The most willing host nations go first. Among them, impact studies favor sites that minimize environmental and social harm, deliver the most value per site and can plug into existing rail, power, water and built infrastructure. Competition to volunteer makes enthusiasm—not favoritism—the entry filter while the program proves the design, trains crews and exposes early mistakes.

  2. Wave 2 · ramp · ~50 sites

    Years 6–12. Start as the pilot closes, with material production and trained capacity expanding.

  3. Wave 3 · peak · ~80 sites

    Years 10–18. Overlap the ramp and build at full production with a mature supply chain and learning curve.

  4. Wave 4 · finish · ~107 sites

    Years 16–24. Reach maximum efficiency, complete all 257 land cities and roll reusable equipment forward from earlier waves.

Why the waves grow—and why the schedule is 24 years. Building too much too early would swamp global concrete supply. The materials ramp sets the early pace. Learning is not held for a clean pause between waves: lessons accumulate in motion, as crews build, correct and keep following the founder. The doubled timeline creates play for shocks and adjustment without pretending the work waits for perfect knowledge. The at least four ocean cities are additive to this land rollout; their schedule and costs are not assigned to these four waves.
140 years 1886 → today
“People ask how long this takes. The automobile took about 140 years to go from Benz's Patent-Motorwagen to reshaping the planet. This project gets about the same — even at half speed.”

The learning curve changes the spend.

Applying an approximate 10% per-land-city cost reduction with each wave to the doubled $28–82T land-city physical-project bracket shifts more sites into later, cheaper production. The at least four additive ocean cities are outside this bracket. The figures below are rounded phase allocations, not audited budgets.

02 / PHYSICAL BASELINE

The current footprint math.

The previous disc, ring and tier layouts have been replaced. The new baseline starts from 6.5 m square floor plates, three stories, and one resident per floor-level unit.

7.7 kmresidential diameter

Residential buildings alone occupy about 46.5 km².

The geometry is direct: one 6.5 × 6.5 m floor is 42.25 m². Spread across three stories, the ground footprint is 14.08 m² per resident. Multiply by 3.3 million residents and convert the resulting area to an equivalent circle.

42.25 ÷ 314.08 m² footprint per person
× 3.3M≈ 46.5 km² residential area
2√(A/π)≈ 7.7 km diameter
Not the finished city edge. Streets, utilities, schools, hospitals, industry, parks, logistics and buffers are excluded, so a real site's diameter must be larger.
The quarry becomes the city site—and feeds the ocean restoration track. Mountain sites are quarried for aggregate, then the prepared, leveled ground becomes the future city footprint. Material extraction and site preparation are one operation rather than two separate landscape scars. Quarrying beyond the 257 land cities' aggregate demand supplies Plan #42's at least four additive ocean cities. Those ocean cities are for Mother Nature—not residents, credits or a second society. Land houses humanity; the ocean track heals the sea.
03 / DEMOGRAPHIC LENS

The cohort sets 257 land cities. The ocean adds four.

At 3 million 14–19-year-olds per land city, today's roughly 770–775 million youth cohort fills about 257–259 land cities. Plan #42 fixes the current land network at 257 and adds at least four ocean cities, bringing the current project total to 261. A separate nonbinding planning set preserves land options for host-nation selection and future reassessment as populations, regions and infrastructure change.

04 / ECONOMICS

The 257-land-city physical baseline costs ~$28–82T.

Physical construction for the 257 land cities is estimated at roughly $28T in the infrastructure-leveraged case and $82T in the fully standalone greenfield case. The at least four additive ocean cities are part of the 261-site project but remain outside this land-derived bracket until their designs are costed. A distinct $3–8T global-compute line covers governance infrastructure, data-center capacity and last-mile connectivity for all 8.2 billion people. Both sit inside one 3%-of-global-GDP bootstrap budget; the contribution ends as cities become self-sufficient. The 75-year frame and 8–24-year build range are arbitrary working figures used to test feasibility—not commitments or promises.

~$28–82T

Physical construction across the 257 land cities: about $28T where infrastructure can be leveraged and about $82T for a standalone greenfield build. The at least four ocean cities are additive and not yet priced. The $3–8T compute layer is a distinct line inside the same 3% bootstrap envelope.

The true 257-land-city physical total stays a bracket because 257 land locations carry 257 different conditions. Existing grids, rail, water, geology, labor and permitting vary too much for one solid figure; site audits refine each local answer without pretending the whole land network collapses to a single universal cost. The leveraged physical case is roughly $28T and the standalone greenfield case roughly $82T. The at least four additive ocean cities remain unpriced. Nuclear remains the dominant site-level line item at $80–160B per greenfield land city; hybrid-airship fleets, edge fields and the carbon-capture loop remain unpriced. The $3–8T compute layer is governance infrastructure inside the same 3% bootstrap budget. That 3% is load-bearing during construction, then ends as self-sufficient city economies take over non-student salaries, maintenance and supplies. If the money never comes, the schools fail: the project owns that failure, tells the next generation “we failed; you do better,” and passes the mandate on. Prestige rivalry is the political engine—nations compete over contributions, hosting and completed cities rather than funding the network through altruism alone.

THE NERVOUS SYSTEM

Global compute is governance infrastructure.

Compute keeps its own $3–8T line for legibility, but it sits inside the same 3%-of-global-GDP bootstrap budget as construction. It is one global-capacity program serving all 8.2 billion people—not a per-site allowance or a second funding ask. Its city facilities run the network-wide class-credit blockchain, with the AI layer maintaining operations.

Separate cost line, one budget. The $3–8T global nervous system is not a per-site cost or a wave allocation; it is governance infrastructure paid from the same 3% bootstrap envelope as the physical project.

Gross project cost is not net cost.

Plan #42 would also avoid or replace spending on slum upgrading, disaster rebuilding, duplicated sprawl infrastructure and public-health costs tied to overcrowding. The direction of those offsets is clear; their magnitude remains open research and is not deducted from the ~$28–82T 257-land-city physical-project bracket. The $3–8T compute program remains separately legible inside the same 3% bootstrap budget. After self-sufficiency, city economies carry salaries for non-students, maintenance and supplies—including feed for the food system.

04A / HEAR-TS STORM ECONOMICS

HEAR-TS Hurricane Suppression — Costs & World Savings (Fermi estimates — ranges, not promises)

What hurricanes cost the world now

  • US hurricanes: ~$90B/yr average, 2016–2024 (29 billion-dollar tropical storms, $820B total — costliest 9-year stretch on record, NOAA/Climate Central).
  • Global tropical cyclones: $135B in 2024 alone (Munich Re); US hurricanes were over $105B of that.
  • Trend: 2020–2025 averaged $147B/yr across ALL US weather disasters vs $55B/yr in 1980–2019 (Climate Central).
  • Lives: 4,026 US deaths from 29 storms, 2016–2024. The top few storms dominate the bill (Helene ~$78B, Milton ~$35B, both 2024).
What it costs

Key framing: the hulls are already being built. The 12.9M-craft HEAR-TS fleet is the transport fleet (moving people, not a hurricane program). The hurricane mission rides on hulls that exist anyway — so the honest cost is the marginal hurricane kit + seasonal operations, not the hulls.

  • Base hull (sunk — transport fleet): $20–50M/craft, ~$35M midpoint. Already budgeted under the fleet goal.
  • Hurricane kit per hull (retrofit): $2–5M/hull. Deep-water pump + riser OR misting/spray gear + sensors + station-keeping upgrades; deck-scale equipment, best hull-fit method.
  • Pilot task force: 10k hulls → $20–50B kit, one-time. Seasonal Atlantic genesis corridors; field-experiment scale.
  • Full Atlantic season: ~1M hulls → $2–5T kit, one-time. Staged over 20 years at 0.1°C increments; Jun–Nov Atlantic, hulls rotate to W. Pacific typhoon season.
  • Annual ops (full season): ~$0.5–1T/yr. Hydrogen fuel, maintenance, crews (~$0.5–1M/hull/yr); mothership/maintenance support shared with the transport fleet.
  • 100k airship delivery layer: cost TBD. Carriers for spraying/seeding/sensing — best delivery layer in the set, solves no physics problems.

What we're NOT buying: new hulls for this mission, ocean-blanket plastic fields (~25 Mt plastic/patch — non-starter), submarine churn.

WHAT THE WORLD SAVES

Keep systems below CAT 4.

Mechanism: don't eliminate storms — stage the cooling 0.1°C at a time over 20 years, keep systems below CAT 4 (bring CAT 4+ down to CAT 3 or weaker). Damage scales roughly with wind speed cubed — a CAT 4 → CAT 3 conversion (~16% wind cut) cuts that storm's damage ~40%. The biggest storms are most of the annual bill, so capping the top end moves the total disproportionately.

  • US avoided damage: ~$30–50B/yr (~$90B/yr baseline; top-end storms capped at CAT 3).
  • Global avoided damage: ~$50–80B/yr (scales from $135B global tropical-cyclone losses in 2024; grows as climate intensifies storms).
  • Lives: hundreds to low thousands/yr.
  • Non-dollar: displacement avoided, food systems spared, FEMA-scale response costs down.

Payback honesty:

At full-season scale, $2–5T kit + ~$0.5–1T/yr ops against $30–80B/yr avoided damage does NOT pay back on dollars alone for a long time. The dollar case is lives + the hulls being sunk cost; the financial case sharpens as climate pushes storm costs up (baseline already 3× the 1980–2019 average). Pilot scale is an experiment, not a savings program — savings arrive in the 2030s–2040s as the task force scales.

The honest part

The fleet makes intervention possible. It does not settle the physics, side effects, law or value case.

1. Hlywiak ceiling:

even perfect, instant, free cooling weakens a storm at most ~15% — the fleet makes the intervention possible, not automatically worthwhile.

2. Staged, not sudden:

0.1°C increments over 20 years so side effects surface early and cheap; termination shock if abandoned mid-season.

3. Steering is the separate, unproven track:

asymmetric nudge is cheap but smaller than forecast error; whoever steers owns the landfall — liability maximal, no legal framework.

4. Ecology + governance:

upwelling risks (HABs, deoxygenation, CO₂ outgassing) unquantified at scale; no international authority exists for cross-border storm intervention.

5. Energy fate unmodeled:

a weakened storm's energy stays in the ocean/atmosphere — where it goes next is an open question.

05 / SITE-SELECTION SCAFFOLD

A planning scaffold. Host nations decide.

The downloadable 810-row ranking is an analytical suggestion set used to test feasibility—not a mandate, a preselected map or a prestige table. Its status hierarchy stays parked until per-site studies are complete. Devolution stands: each host nation chooses its own locations from that suggestion set, guided by studies that weigh the least environmental and social impact against the most value each site can deliver. Existing rail, power, water, buildings and industrial capacity count in that value—especially for the first wave. Too many variables differ by location for one solid audit answer; the cost bracket is the honest output.

06 / SYSTEMS SOLUTIONS

A working city spine.

Movement, freight, trade, food, water, power and construction-carbon recovery now connect as one planning architecture. The system has clear roles and handoffs; its capacity and site-specific engineering still need to be proven.

People above. Freight below and beyond.

A layered ground network keeps each mode doing one job well, while Airlander-style hybrid airships add a regional air bridge where rail is incomplete or disrupted.

Car-free, not road-free.Narrow emergency and service lanes remain. Maintenance and compact emergency vehicles stay golf-cart-sized; there are no private cars, arterials or parking fields.

Still to size: passenger headways, pod capacity, edge-terminal throughput and construction-phase logistics before the tunnels exist.

01 / TOP

Light rail

A dense passenger network across the 7.7 km disc, targeting roughly 15 minutes end to end.

people
02 / BELOW

Autonomous electric pods

Underground rail or maglev freight on radial spokes of about 4 km, running from edge terminals toward the center.

local freight
03 / EDGE

Heavy rail

Bulk food, goods and construction material arrive from outside at terminals around the disc edge.

regional freight
04 / AIR

Hybrid airships

Airlander-style aircraft bridge remote sites, broken rail corridors and urgent regional supply gaps from dedicated landing and mooring fields at the edge.

air bridge
Edge handoffHeavy rail or airship → edge terminal → underground pods → local distribution

The edge is also the trade gateway.

Each terminal combines intermodal transfer, bonded warehousing and customs clearance at one controlled perimeter. Heavy rail forms the trunk network; hybrid airships provide an alternate regional link where rail is absent, unfinished or temporarily cut.

ImportsBulk staples, construction materials and manufactured goods arrive by rail, sea and air, with service roads as a fourth route.
ExportsManufactured output and surplus food move back onto the same multimodal network.
Inter-site tradeHeavy rail carries trunk freight; shipping serves coastal access; airships bridge broken corridors; service roads, go-kart tracks and bike paths take freight in a pinch.
A siege has to cut every route at once. Rail, sea, air and service-road access are deliberately independent, and inside the city every paved surface—including go-kart tracks and bike paths—becomes freight capacity in an emergency. No single cutoff can starve a city; a blockade has to sever the whole multimodal web.

Still to design: customs jurisdiction, bonded-zone rules, terminal ownership, inspection capacity, cross-border interoperability, port interfaces, airship fleet size, weather limits, and landing and mooring fields.

7.7 kmdisc inside
utility belt

Three protein pillars, built into one local food loop.

Each city needs about 60,000 tonnes of protein a year. Plan #42 sizes three production pillars to 72,000 tonnes—120% of need—so the system carries a deliberate buffer while moat aquaculture, peri-urban poultry and indoor crickets share local feed and fertilizer loops.

It reads as a moat; it works as a utility belt. The saltwater ring is not a fortification. It is shared infrastructure for fish farming and the doubled hatchery, desalination intake, evaporation, recreation, district heating and cooling, and thermal-energy storage. The closed path also supports continuous water circulation: oxygenating the hatchery, carrying waste toward treatment, protecting desalination intake quality and preventing stagnation. The ring is simply the most efficient shape—maximum utility and continuous flow per meter of moat. Form follows function, not fortification. In the end, though, a roughly 100 m ring of water around a sovereign city can function as a fortification whether it was designed as one or not: that defense is emergent, not intended—dual-use by geometry, not by doctrine.
72,000 t/yeartotal protein capacity across all three pillars
120% of need20% buffer for spoilage, growth and trade
Moat fish · ~35%~21,000 t protein from ~96,000 t whole fish per year; doubled food hatchery, entirely for consumption.
Poultry · ~45%~27,000 t protein from about 50 million broilers per year plus about 6 million laying hens in the farm belt.
Crickets · ~40%~24,000 t protein from about 120,000 t live crickets per year in roughly 1.5 km² of stacked indoor vertical facilities.
The 20% buffer is working capacity, not excess. It absorbs spoilage, supports population growth and creates a trade margin when another site's production falls short.
Survival first; no ocean release program. All hatchery output is raised for food. Juvenile survival through hatchery and grow-out is the binding fish-production constraint: improving survival multiplies harvested protein from every batch far more efficiently than adding eggs alone.

The world feeds the cities' animals; the graduates feed the world. Imported feed is the outside world's material stake in Plan #42. Local crop residues, plant waste and nutrient recovery reduce that import burden but do not pretend it disappears. In return, graduates carry skilled labor back into the wider world while the cities return energy, knowledge and manufactured output. The doubled hatchery's capital cost, poultry and cricket biosecurity, exact feed volumes, farm-belt land mix and moat exchange still need site-by-site engineering.

The saltwater ring is a utility belt. The cities become energy anchors.

Fish production, the doubled hatchery, desalination intake, evaporation, recreation, district heating and cooling, and thermal-energy storage share the perimeter system; defense is not its purpose. Continuous circulation oxygenates the fish system, moves waste toward treatment, protects desalination intake quality and prevents stagnation. It rings the city because a ring delivers maximum utility and uninterrupted flow per meter of moat. A mixed energy portfolio keeps each city from depending on one source. Across the 257 land cities, the buildout reaches roughly 2.6 TW: intentionally large enough to help remake world energy generation and use, with the cities acting as reliable anchor customers—not a hidden utility cost.

04 / WATER

Desalination from the moat

There is no single moat-water answer. Coastal sites can draw seawater; inland sites may use a pipeline or manufacture brine, with the local audit choosing the fit. Water then enters a dedicated treatment train, becomes potable water and moves into a citywide reuse loop. Concentrated brine stays out of the fish habitat; useful salts go to molten-salt reactor systems and sodium-based batteries, while Plan #42's at least four additive, uninhabited ocean cities redisperse the remainder.

moat intake→desalination→potable loop+brine feedstock

Per-site answer: audit daily demand, intake and replenishment, storage, wastewater recovery, salt recovery and transport, safe ocean redispersion and whether the local source is coastal, piped or manufactured brine. The variability is real; no single network-wide moat-water design is claimed.

05 / ENERGY

A ~2.6 TW global energy program

Nuclear supplies firm generation for round-the-clock city loads and desalination. Solar and wind add distributed power when conditions allow; storage and the grid balance the portfolio. At network scale, that generation build is a core product of Plan #42: the cities create dependable demand that can finance and accelerate a cleaner, larger world energy system.

Nuclearfirm core supply
Solardaytime generation
Windsite-dependent generation
Fusionfuture option, not baseline
The switch is entirely on the host's side of the meter. The city powers itself first, then offers its surplus to the host. A host that permits the reactor can turn off its own lights—stop drawing that export—but the switch cannot touch the city, its generation, essential systems or government. Everything inside continues unchanged; when the host draws, the surplus flows outward.

Core selling point, not a buried cost: the planned ~2.6 TW buildout is meant to fix more than city power. Site audits still have to size peak load, reactor count and type, renewable area, storage duration, grid redundancy, cooling and waste management.

06 / CONSTRUCTION CARBON

Capture the build's carbon. Feed the growing system.

Construction will still create major emissions, especially through cement and steel. Capture equipment at material plants and temporary energy systems would separate usable CO₂ instead of treating every tonne as an unavoidable release. The usable share feeds indoor crops; their plant waste becomes feed for co-located cricket farms.

CaptureCollect concentrated CO₂ from cement, steel and construction-phase energy where technically practical.
ConditionPurify and meter a food-grade stream for controlled-environment agriculture.
Grow, feed or storeUse only what indoor crops can absorb; route plant waste to cricket farms, then mineralize or permanently store the remaining CO₂.
material production→CO₂ capture→indoor plants→cricket feed+mineral storage

Not a full offset by itself. Indoor plant demand is limited and captured CO₂ returns to the atmosphere when plants or crickets are eaten. Permanent storage, lower-carbon materials and clean construction power remain necessary; each site's source, purity, transport, crop demand and cricket-feed safety still need engineering.

07 / WHERE THE HOLES STAND

Answers added. Contradictions stay visible.

Rounds 16–17 close the political ignition, adult transition, founding credential price, rollout-speed and naming questions. The register below is deliberately unresolved: these problems still change how Plan #42 would work, so they are not buried as implementation detail.

Open · unresolved

Ten seams still need answers.

Nine are design holes. One is intentionally left to the first generation. Closing a neighboring problem does not close the one named here.

01 · Ledger finality

Credits are said to be “destroyed” at cashout, yet the blockchain is immutable. A burn address leaves them visible; a tombstone records an instruction to ignore them. Destruction versus finality remains contradictory.

02 · ROI geography

The host pays land and pre-education while its young people scatter across 257 land cities and graduates may work anywhere. The plan still lacks a return address for the host’s investment.

03 · Games organizer

The annual 257-land-venue carnival games and World Cup-sized audience have a format, but no institution has been designed to schedule, govern and operate them.

04 · Pre-education staffing

Hosts carry a funded duty to prepare roughly 770 million young people, but the teaching corps does not exist on paper. Who teaches the operating language and life skills remains unanswered.

05 · The conveyor belt

About 2.1 million people turn 14 each day worldwide. Intake is a constant flow, not a neat cohort; batch-designed sorting, housing, teaching and graduation systems may break.

06 · The 99% rubber stamp

If the AI earns near-perfect audit weight, human override becomes the suspicious anomaly. The “eyes, not hands” boundary can dissolve into de facto machine rule under its own success.

07 · The hostage flip

The host cannot switch off the reactor, but it still controls land, rail access and supply routes. The light-switch answer did not resolve the more practical chokepoints.

08 · Staff’s young children

The 300,000 randomized adults may have children under 14. Their housing, schooling, care and relationship to the city remain undesigned.

09 · Specialist engineering

Construction methods, moat hydrology, grid architecture, terminal throughput, airship pricing and waste endpoints still require site-specific engineering.

Open by design · what counts as “partial” service.

The first generation defines the threshold and meaning of partial service; the founding plan will not decide it for them.

Why people come

A new bridge school replaces the final years of K–12 and begins before higher education, giving each site an educational anchor.

Where work happens

The city is multi-story and mixed-use—not a single-story residential dormitory. Employment and production are part of the vertical program.

Who builds it

Builders construct a place they can stay in, then continue building so they and later arrivals can stay longer.

What gets rebuilt

Every site begins with a scrap-versus-keep audit: reuse sound infrastructure, replace what fails the new plan and build greenfield only where needed.

How the rollout scales

Start with the 20 most willing volunteer hosts, then grow through waves of roughly 50, 80 and 107 sites. Lessons accumulate in motion while the project follows the founder; the doubled 24-year schedule leaves room for correction without requiring each wave to stop and wait.

Why the building never ends

The 24-year timeline constructs the network; incoming cohorts keep it. Perpetual refurbishment is a feature because every new generation needs meaningful work: each cohort repairs, renews and rebuilds the cities it inherits.

What happens to build carbon

Capture CO₂ during material production and construction; feed the usable share to indoor plant growth, then mineralize or store the balance.

Where the aggregate comes from

Quarry mountain sites for construction material, then build on the prepared ground. The quarry operation and future city-site preparation are the same job.

Why the energy scale is so large

The roughly 2.6 TW network buildout is intentional: the cities are anchor customers for a program meant to improve world energy generation and use.

What the host's light switch controls

Only the host's own draw. A host can stop importing a city's surplus power, but it cannot switch off the city, its generation, essential systems or government.

Why the city has a moat

The saltwater ring is functional infrastructure for fish, desalination, evaporation, circulation, recreation and thermal-energy storage. Students tend its hatchery ecology as curriculum: stewardship is humanity’s responsibility taught by practice. Any defensive effect is emergent geometry, not the design intent or doctrine.

Where desalination brine goes

Brine is feedstock, not waste. Plan #42's at least four additive, uninhabited ocean cities redisperse what cannot be used; recovered salts feed molten-salt reactor systems and sodium-based batteries. The ocean track serves Mother Nature—no residents and no credits.

Who feeds whom

The outside world contributes animal feed; alumni return skilled labor to the wider economy. The material input and human return form one social compact.

How supply resilience starts

Independent rail, sea, air and service-road links reduce dependence on a single route; in an emergency, go-kart tracks and bike paths become local freight routes. Host control of land and supply corridors still remains open in the hostage-flip problem.

How daily value moves

Class credits are born networked: one ledger and one tally of total earned, spendable only inside all 257 land cities. At exit, the school is the single buyer. The intended cashout is terminal and nothing enters a secondary market, but how an immutable ledger records true destruction remains open.

What the stock does—and cannot do

The stock signals completed work to an employer or university; the full signal requires graduation. Its only sale is the resident’s exit cashout back to the school. Universities handle admission and placement. There is no secondary market: legible, never liquid. The first generation defines what qualifies as partial service.

Why teacher power is not new

Teachers already grade students, exercise classroom command and influence rewards. Plan #42 makes the hierarchy explicit but does not require uniforms or invent a new concentration of power.

Why graduate absorption is not a new shock

High schools already release millions of graduates into economies every year. Plan #42 makes the flow bigger and more coordinated, but labor markets already absorb this kind of annual transition; the scale changes, not the category.

Who controls the ledger

The ledger is a blockchain maintained through a defined waterfall: facilities → interlayer → AI → graduate auditors → host nation. City compute infrastructure runs it; the interlayer checks the facilities; the AI layer checks and maintains network operation; graduates audit the AI's logic and records; and the host has read-only basement access. Physical and logical controls let the host watch without the ability to grab, alter or operate the system. No single minter and no single watcher can capture it.

How pre-education works

Nations redirect roughly the final two years of existing K–12 spending into preparation. There are no one-shot rejects: residents repeat until ready. Those who still cannot meet the standard are sent home, and send-back rates—before and after city intake—diagnose what the teaching system must fix.

What pre-education teaches

Adult life skills, not book knowledge: the operating language, shop, welding, house building, nutrition and the other practical work people face at 20 and beyond. Nations teach their kids how to live; the cities teach them the rest after intake. Pre-education needs no one-size-fits-all central academic curriculum.

How local languages survive

Intake begins at 14, after children have spent their formative years living and learning in their local languages. Their mother tongues are fully formed before the cities introduce an operating language as a late-learned second language, not a replacement. The intake age is the language-preservation design.

Who writes and audits the operator

Graduates, the host nation and the UN-esque governing body jointly author the AI charter and objective function. The charter also contains breakdown rules pre-agreed by all three layers, so collapse or deadlock in one layer does not force improvisation. The host watches through enforced read-only access; the governing body operates; graduates audit.

What the host bargain offers

Host nations trade land and jurisdiction for educated graduates, energy and a seat in the feed loop. The offer is legible, but which graduates or benefits return to the host that paid remains open as the ROI-geography problem.

Who administers the founding vote

The current UN runs the first referendum among the nations that agree to participate, using its member-state machinery, observers and institutional legitimacy. The willing vote first, just as the willing host first; the UN's last great act is administering the vote that creates its UN-esque successor.

What “real” student power means

Local councils hold binding authority over dorms, schedules and daily life, while a general assembly of cities works as a mini UN for network-wide student representation. Reactors, grids, water systems and other existential infrastructure stay under professional control.

What leaving means

Exit is repatriation. The resident's home nation takes responsibility after return; the city's duty and jurisdiction end at the border. Reciprocity enforces the handoff: a nation that refuses its returnees is cut off from sending new intake.

How culture travels

Culture and religion are shared rather than imposed. Residents bring them in, exchange them and carry a wider shared culture home after graduation.

What the “war” games are

Annual inter-school carnival competitions—go-kart racing, laser tag and other games of skill—with a World Cup-sized audience and a year between editions. All 257 land cities serve as rotating venues. The “war” is entirely in quotes; the organizer remains undesigned.

What the provisional ranking means

Nothing about prestige yet. The 810-row order is planning scaffolding, and its status hierarchy stays parked until per-site studies replace spreadsheet position with evidenced fit.

Ranking prestige is parked until the studies are complete.

Host nations choose their own sites from the 810-row suggestion set; no location earns status from a provisional spreadsheet position. Per-site studies compare viable options for the least environmental and social harm and the most value delivered, weighing land, ecology, hazards, communities, cultural sites and livelihoods alongside existing rail, grid, water, buildings and industrial capacity. First-wave pilots should plug into as much working infrastructure as possible. The ranking informs those studies; it does not impose a global selection or settle a hierarchy. Audits refine each site separately, but too many local variables exist for one solid global answer; the ~$28–82T 257-land-city bracket is honesty, not a placeholder pretending uniformity.

Work already assigned.

These briefs continue in parallel. They do not replace the unresolved design register above.

Prioritize existing capacity in the first wave.
  • Institution designersBuild the anchor school by consulting China and adapting lessons from the world’s largest education system to a 3-million-student city. The institutional form still needs design, but the starting point is proven scale—not invention from zero. The external contribution closes as each city becomes self-sufficient.

Conscription school.

Universal service, where the service is education. Each site is a 3.3-million-person education-centered city: roughly 3 million residents aged 14–19, supported by 300,000 adults aged 30 and older. The rank structure organizes learning, care and operations without creating a separate military caste.

3Mresidents aged 14–19 · the resident majority
SUPPORTED BY
300Kadults aged 30+ · educators, carers, operators and civic staff

The human pipeline closes the loop.

Plan #42 treats intake, staffing, graduation, oversight and failure recovery as one operating system. A new parallel institution coordinates it: UN-esque in multinational, mandate-based form, but not the existing UN and not a UN-reform project. It is purpose-built with the capacity the plan requires. Member states supply the adult capacity; alumni become both the project's return to the world and the network's renewable civic reserve.

Three stages, two graduate exits

Host nations deliver pre-education before intake: operating language, shop, welding, house building, nutrition and other practical skills. There are no one-shot rejects—repeat until ready. If readiness still is not reached, the resident is sent home. Conscription school follows, then graduates exit through work or higher education. The lifecycle otherwise follows today's colleges: intake, study, completion and exit.

Departure is the system's diagnostic

Send-back rates before intake diagnose pre-education; exits after intake diagnose the city school. Every departure identifies where language support, teaching, care or operations must improve. The pipeline recycles before it releases, then learns from each release.

Repatriation is reciprocal

A home nation that refuses its returnees loses the privilege of sending new residents into the network. Intake remains open only while return remains open: the pipeline is two-way or it closes for that nation.

77 million adults begin as scaffolding

Member states contribute teachers, engineers, clinicians and operators to maintain the cities at the start. Students absorb operations as curriculum, the AI absorbs coordination and graduates replace the rest; the adult footprint shrinks as the network learns what it can do without them.

Cold start is a resource dial

Wave 1 must turn directed money, people, materials and political will into visible graduates, energy and prestige fast. The “go” is distributed uniformly by population density so no region leapfrogs another; starve the launch and the waiting queue becomes the risk.

A purpose-built construction corps

The new institution's dedicated multinational corps mobilizes construction labor across all four waves, rolling trained people and equipment from one build phase into the next. After the 24-year network build, refurbishment becomes permanent student work: each incoming cohort repairs and rebuilds the cities it inherits.

Biosecurity through network redundancy

An outbreak triggers city-scale quarantine. The other 256 land cities absorb displaced population, production and essential functions; resilience belongs to the network, not one supposedly fail-proof city.

Three parties author the AI charter

Graduates, the host nation and the UN-esque governing body jointly write the AI's objective function and pre-agree the charter's own breakdown rules. Graduates audit its logic and outcomes; the host gets physically and logically enforced read-only access—watch without grab—while the governing body operates it. Any ordinary charter change still requires all three.

Receivership for failed cities

A city that cannot govern or operate safely enters receivership led by the outside world's contributed workforce together with the alumni network.

Generational legitimacy is the familiar problem

The founding mandate faces no different capture risk than today's institutions. Re-ratification remains held in reserve if a later generation rejects the compact, but it is not built in as a constant destabilizer. The working assumption is that future residents will be okay with the inherited system while retaining a constitutional route to revisit it.

AI in 42

To be reviewed · drafted, not decided, awaiting review

One mind. One memory. One charter. Local faces. One unified AI operates across all 257 land cities, expressed through a local face for each land city and school. It is never 257 competing instances: competing minds would fork the charter, optimize for their own cities, hoard advantage and break the even deal.

01 · Maintain the class-credit ledger

With the facilities and interlayer, the AI maintains the network-wide class-credit blockchain and its operation. It keeps one coherent record across all 257 land cities while graduate auditors inspect its logic and records.

02 · Balance the network

It tracks populations and resources, schedules movement and capacity, knows what is needed and what is extra, and matches needs with surpluses city to city. One shared operating picture keeps 257 land-city pressures from becoming 257 competing systems.

03 · Be the sorting hat

Assignment is not a blind day-one lottery. The AI spends a full year assessing each student, then assigns students to schools while preserving the even deal and balanced shares of talent across the network.

04 · Teach the person, not the average

It learns how each student learns, then explains each concept in the way that specific person needs in order to understand and retain it. Human faculty teach the many; the AI adapts the explanation to the one.

05 · Be the reminder

It schedules spaced repetition around each student’s forgetting curve and nudges at the right moment—before the lesson fades, not after it is gone. The reminder is the forgetting curve’s enemy.

Measurement, never judgment

The AI does not touch final grades, discipline decisions, mentorship or the boost decision. Humans judge. The AI measures, checks and audits, then leaves consequential decisions in human hands.

Eyes, not hands

An audit flag goes to the human in charge, is visible to the person being audited, is logged and remains non-binding. The AI cannot execute the consequence attached to its own flag; graduates audit the audit itself.

Weight is earned, not assigned — boundary unresolved

A public hit rate calibrates trust in the AI’s flags and recommendations, scaled by stakes. Its weight may rise to 99%, never 100%; whether that makes human review a de facto rubber stamp remains open.

Set for purpose, not power. Administrator, sorter, tutor, reminder and auditor—not ruler. Its importance may grow only through accuracy, transparency and ownership of error: wider eyes, never hands. This entire charter is TBD—drafted, not decided, awaiting review.

The resident compact.

Daily life links learning, value, movement and identity without pretending that a multilingual, multi-faith population will become culturally uniform.

Class credits are born networked; exit is intended to be terminal

Coursework, service and merit feed one total-earned tally spendable only inside the 257 land cities. Graduation converts the balance into the full completion-reward stock; early exit can convert at a lower number. No secondary market follows, but whether immutable credits end at a burn address or a tombstone is still unresolved.

The stock identifies; the world boosts

Nothing special happens for genius inside the school: the even deal holds through graduation, with no privileged track. Completion is required for the full signal. After school, the stock identifies exceptional work and universities, employers and the wider world provide the boost.

The stock is legible, never liquid

The only sale occurs at exit, when the school buys the credits back and converts them into completion-reward stock. No employer or third party can buy, transfer, collateralize or speculate on it. The number expresses the graduate's value to an employer or university—not the market value of a stock.

The ledger expects devils

Because one ledger holds both academic record and economic power, it runs through a fixed waterfall: facilities → interlayer → AI → graduate auditors → host. Trust and authority cascade in that order, and every downstream layer checks the one above. There is no single minter or single watcher to capture.

Intake at 14 preserves the mother tongue

Children spend their first 14 years living and learning in local languages, so those languages are fully formed before the cities touch them. The operating language arrives through pre-education as a late-learned second language, not a replacement. The intake age is the preservation mechanism.

Higher education owns placement

The pipeline is pre-education → conscription school → work or higher education. The stock is the signal; universities and programs make their own admissions decisions. After that handoff, the lifecycle follows current colleges.

Exit means repatriation—and reciprocity

A resident may leave, but departure returns responsibility to the home nation. If that nation refuses its returnees, it cannot send new intake; the pipeline is two-way or it is closed.

Culture is exchanged

Residents bring their cultures and religions, share them without an imposed replacement and carry the resulting shared culture home as graduates.

Diversity is the mechanism

Difference is not treated as a problem to manage. Cross-cultural exchange is one of the network's intended outputs.

Staff’s young children remain open

Randomized adults may arrive with children under 14, while the city’s learning system begins at 14. Housing, schooling, care and whether families remain together have not been designed.

Round 13–14: scale, equality and the seams.

The newest answers define how the school borrows proven scale, how the network stays even, where the AI stops, and how the credential and annual games meet the outside world.

Pedagogy starts with China

At 3 million students per city, Plan #42 consults China and adapts the world’s largest education system rather than inventing mass pedagogy from scratch.

Accreditation comes with time

National education ministries and international bodies provide the first recognition. The network earns its own standing by operating, graduating cohorts and producing a record the world can evaluate.

Educator-corps politics are familiar

Promotion, span of control and bureaucratic drift are not the education sector’s biggest unknowns. Plan #42 makes familiar institutional problems larger; it does not make them novel.

Every city gets the same hand

Students and staff are randomized and balanced across all 257 land cities, including equalized shares of top performers. No city can become the premium or discount version of the network.

The alumni bloc is a future question

Ask their kids when they come through in X years. The plan does not pre-write the politics of its descendants; future cohorts inherit the vote and answer for themselves.

The AI is administrator, not ruler

It keeps track, schedules, balances people across 257 land cities, matches needs with surpluses and knows what is needed versus extra. It does not set law, allocate rights or hold political authority.

Moat ecology is schoolwork

Humanity’s responsibility for the moat is taught in the curriculum. Students tend hatchery ecosystems, monitor invasive species and algae, and learn stewardship by doing it.

Partial credit is left to the first generation

A resident who exits early may cash out below the full completion reward, but the founding plan does not define the threshold or meaning of “partial.” The first generation decides what service counts.

Genius waits until after school

The even deal holds through graduation: no special track or boost inside the school. Completion is required; then the stock identifies exceptional work and universities, employers and the wider world provide the boost.

The network sets how; the host sets what

The network owns methods, procedures and operational limits. The host owns meaning, narrative and local content. These are different axes: shared verbs, local nouns.

Fast proof closes the envy queue

Wave 1 must make graduates, energy and prestige visible quickly enough that later waves see results rather than promises. Cold-start speed depends on how much is directed at “go,” distributed uniformly by population density so no region leapfrogs another.

The games travel every year

Plan for a World Cup-sized audience and an annual competition with a year between editions. All 257 land cities become venues, rotating the host spotlight across the network instead of building one permanent stage.

Round 15: endure the mess, keep the surplus flowing, name the teams.

Three administrative seams now have answers. None needs a grand new institution before the network can move; one is survived, one is judged by delivery and one starts simple.

The charter’s language: time and a shitshow

Translating the AI charter, ledger contracts and student constitution across 190+ nations becomes a permanent legal and version-control bureaucracy. Amendments bring mistranslations, version drift and amendment chaos. There is no clean mechanism pretending that away: the answer is endurance, correction and time until the versions converge.

Energy metering: judge the surplus by whether it arrives

No elaborate trusted meter is needed while surplus power reaches the host nation. The arrangement runs on rough justice: the surplus flows, the host’s lights stay on and everyone is satisfied. Aging host plants can be mothballed into reserve as city surplus replaces their normal output; precision matters only if delivery stops.

School naming stays human

The Color + Animal system was an AI proposal, not a naming decision. People name the 257 land schools and choose their banners, colors and identities. The AI may measure duplication or balance; it does not judge the names.

Rounds 16–17: ignition, scaffolding and proof.

Five questions now have direct operating answers. They close the sales, transition, price-discovery, rollout and naming seams without erasing the open register above.

Political coordination sells through rivalry

The envy window is the ignition, the measuring contest the fuel and duty to humanity the public cover. The most willing volunteers sign first; rivals follow because no leader wants to sit outside while another nation builds cities.

The 300,000 adults are scaffolding

They maintain each city while the network learns what can be done without them. Students absorb operations as curriculum, the AI absorbs coordination and graduates replace the remaining roles. The adult footprint shrinks as learning accumulates.

Founding stock uses a posted union scale

The credential works like a union apprenticeship, not an IPO. As the monopoly issuer, the network declares the scale the way plumbers’ and electricians’ unions post journeyman rates. The first price is posted, not discovered in a vacuum.

Fast, uniform “go” turns waiting into proof

Wave 1 must show graduates, energy and prestige quickly. Cold-start speed is a dial set by money, people, materials and political will; the launch scales with population density so regions advance together rather than leapfrogging one another.

People name the schools

Color + Animal was an AI suggestion only. People choose the names, colors, banners and identities. The operating boundary holds here too: measurement, never judgment.

Enemy’s lens: name the charge, answer the structure.

These answers do not ask opponents to trust the project’s intentions. They define the limits, flows and local authority that the plan must make observable.

“It’s a cult.”

Sure—so is church, at the level of shape. There are no uniforms in the plan; adults setting doctrine is simply how school works. At succession, the founder becomes dean of one college—a demotion by design, with no throne to inherit. The constitutional backstop remains: every ideology is limited in scope; nothing totalizes.

“It’s colonialism.”

The charge is conceded in shape, then bounded across different axes. The network sets how: methods, procedures and operational limits. The host sets what: meaning, narrative and local content. Shared verbs; local nouns.

“It’s a tax haven.”

The credit flow is one way and cannot loop back on itself. The only inflow is transparent global “tax” revenue, and the network is taxed on surplus received. There are no two-way opaque flows and no laundering circuit.

“It’ll never get the money.”

Then the schools fail. The 3% bootstrap is load-bearing during construction, not forever. If it never arrives, the project says plainly: we failed; you do better. The mandate passes to the next generation instead of being disguised as success.

What makes the politics move

The most willing volunteers sign first. Then prestige rivalry supplies the engine: no leader wants to sit outside while a rival builds cities. The envy window ignites the contest, measuring keeps it fueled and duty to humanity gives it public cover.

“It’s eugenics.”

The stock rewards and sorts completed work; it does not rank human worth. Ideologies are capped so none can totalize, and the pipeline repeats, recycles and uses send-back rates to repair itself rather than selecting people for elimination.

“The students are hostages.”

Parent–teacher conferences, family visits and spring break keep the cities permeable. Residents move between school, home and family life; this is a boarding-school model, not a sealed enclave.

What “military-esque” means

Structure and some discipline only: ranks, hierarchy and order without warfighting, weapons doctrine or a combat mission. There are no weapons, period—no drones, knives, guns or explosives.

INSIDE THE CITY

Conscription school: service through education.

The city uses military-esque organization for universal educational service: structure and some discipline, no more. The cities use ranks, hierarchy and order; they are not a fighting force. There is no warfighting, weapons doctrine or combat mission. There are no weapons—no drones, knives, guns or explosives—and no uniforms are required by the plan. The officer corps is made of educators. Teachers, principals and superintendents already grade, direct and administer rewards in schools today; Plan #42 makes that hierarchy explicit rather than inventing a new power. Duty of care and educational safeguarding travel through the same chain of command.

  • Educators hold command: teachers lead learning units, principals command schools and superintendents coordinate the citywide system.
  • Universal educational service: everyone serves by learning, teaching, caring, building or operating the systems that make education possible.
  • Safeguarding in the hierarchy: advancement depends on educational competence, duty of care, audited performance and the protection of young residents.
  • No weapons, period: no drones, knives, guns or explosives; no warfighting doctrine and no combat mission.
  • Inter-school “war” games: annual carnival competitions—go-kart racing, laser tag and other games of skill—planned for a World Cup-sized audience, with one year between editions. Every city becomes a venue as hosting rotates across all 257 land cities. The “war” is entirely in quotes: these are not combat simulations.
OUTSIDE THE CITY

Sovereign at the negotiating table.

Each city acts as a sovereign entity in external affairs, but sovereignty is a negotiated exchange: the host nation grants land and jurisdiction; the network returns educated graduates, energy and participation in the feed loop.

  • Return on investment: intended to be measured first in graduates, but the geography is unresolved. A host funds land and pre-education while graduates scatter across the network and the wider world; the bargain still needs a return address.
  • Host-nation treaties: define territory, jurisdiction, movement, taxation, utilities, dispute resolution and the terms of the exchange.
  • Exit by repatriation: a departing resident returns to the home nation, which assumes responsibility beyond the city border. A nation that refuses returnees is barred from sending new intake.
  • Bounded sovereignty: the founding treaty states exactly which powers remain with the host nation and which transfer to the city.

Student government scales as a mini UN.

Local councils hold practical authority over dorms, schedules and daily rules. Across the network, a general assembly of cities gives students representation at 257-land-city scale. Reactors, grids, water systems and other existential infrastructure remain behind professional operating and safety boundaries.

Sovereignty is granted through a defined trade.The host nation grants land and jurisdiction; in return it receives graduates, energy and a seat in the feed loop. Full-term graduates receive stock as a completion reward, while its outside valuation records recognition of their work without pricing the people themselves. Its reciprocal obligations are pre-education before intake and accepting its people at repatriation. Pre-education is funded by redirecting roughly two years of existing K–12 spending because the cities absorb those school years; refusing returnees suspends that nation's intake privilege. Without negotiated treaties and durable legal recognition, a city may function at scale but it is not sovereign.

The mayor is superintendent-in-chief.

The job is not merely to manage a workforce and infrastructure. It is to lead an education-centered city of 3 million young residents while protecting them, keeping adult support systems accountable and preserving political legitimacy.

Elected, removable and human.The AI operator keeps track, schedules and balances people and resources across all 257 land cities—knowing what is needed and what is extra. It does not set law, allocate rights, police dissent or hold the mayor’s authority: administrator, not ruler.
A mandate from the youth majority

Voting rules give 14–19-year-olds binding authority over dorms, schedules and other local matters—not merely an advisory role—while existential infrastructure remains under professional operating and safety control.

Adolescent-development fluency

The office needs the instincts of an educator and safeguarding leader alongside the executive skills of a conventional mayor.

Safeguarding at city scale

Independent child-protection oversight, vetted adult roles, confidential reporting, due process and privacy are citywide infrastructure, not a single department.

Fast, credible public communication

Digital participation, published response times and plain-language decisions let 3 million young residents test authority without being patronized.

A workable adult service compact

The 300,000 adults are full citizens whose roles are organized around youth education, health, safety and city operations. Their duties, labor rights and routes to representation must be explicit so support does not become coercion or resentment.

LegitimacyStudent government has binding authority over dorms, schedules and local daily life, with existential infrastructure outside its remit.
AccountabilityThe class-credit blockchain follows a defined waterfall: facilities → interlayer → AI → graduate auditors → host. Each downstream layer checks the one above: no single minter, no single watcher.
Founder succession is demotion by designThe founder becomes dean of one college. There is no throne or network-wide office to inherit; succession narrows authority instead of reproducing it.
08 / CONFIDENCE NOTE

Confidence note.

Design coherence: ~80% — seventeen rounds of hole-poking, most holes closed or owned.

The numbers: ~30% — grossly estimated scaffolding, in-the-lab, not promises.

Execution (politics, 24 years, 261 cities): ~25% — "it sells easy" is faith; history is a graveyard of plans that sold easy and died on coordination.

That something worth having comes out of attempting it: ~85% — even a failed 42 leaves the ledger ideas, the school models, the Fermi work.

The assistant has no internal confidence meter; these percentages are uncalibrated estimates, recorded because the user asked, not because they are trustworthy numbers.

Current baseline

Plan #42 and Project 42 are interchangeable names for the same project. It is a 261-site project: 257 land cities for roughly 770 million residents aged 14–19 and 77 million supporting adults, plus at least four additive, uninhabited ocean cities dedicated to healing the sea. Those adults begin as operating scaffolding; students absorb operations as curriculum, the AI absorbs coordination and graduates progressively replace the rest. The 810-location ranking is a nonbinding suggestion pool; host nations choose sites after local studies, and the first 20 pilots are the most willing volunteers. Because every location brings different land, water, grid, rail, geology and social conditions, per-site audits refine the work without promising one universal answer; the ~$28–82T 257-land-city physical bracket is the honest result. Moat water is likewise local: coastal draw, pipeline or manufactured brine. The anchor school must be built by adapting lessons from China’s large-scale education system, with accreditation earned first through ministries and international bodies and later through its own operating record. Pre-education repeats until residents are ready; when readiness still is not reached, they are sent home, and send-back rates before and after intake diagnose what the system must fix. Infrastructure for staff members’ children under 14 remains undesigned. Parent–teacher conferences, family visits and spring break keep the cities permeable rather than sealed. Student government combines binding local authority over daily life with a network-wide general assembly: a mini UN, while existential infrastructure remains under professional control. The founder eventually becomes dean of one college, a demotion by design with no throne to inherit. Generational capture is the familiar institutional risk; re-ratification is held in reserve rather than imposed continuously. The AI charter and its breakdown rules are pre-agreed by graduates, the host nation and the UN-esque governing body. Ideologies are capped, the pipeline recycles, and stock describes completed work rather than human worth. At exit, the school is the stock's single buyer; there is no secondary market. Its number expresses value to an employer or university, not the market value of the instrument. Higher education owns admissions and placement, and the lifecycle otherwise follows today's colleges. The 3% contribution is a construction bootstrap, not a permanent levy: physical construction and the distinct $3–8T compute-governance layer sit inside one budget. As cities become self-sufficient, their own economies take over non-student salaries, maintenance and supplies, including feed for the food system. The most willing volunteers sign first; prestige rivalry pulls the rest in, while cold-start resources scale with population density. If the money never arrives, the schools fail; the project owns the failure and passes the mandate to the next generation. The four waves learn in motion as the work follows the founder, rather than waiting for a clean extraction pause. The roles stay distinct: the 257 land cities house humanity; the at least four additive, uninhabited ocean cities carry no people or credits and exist for Mother Nature—to heal the sea.
